newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian gold market shrugs off death of China's Deng.
newsitem.headline: Asian gold market shrugs off death of China's Deng.

text.p: Asian gold markets shrugged off the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, focusing instead on robust demand and tight supplies which have sent spot premiums soaring, bullion dealers said on Thursday.

"(Deng) has been out of it for so long that nobody thought there would be any impact," said Dick Gazmararian, executive vice president of Asia Pacific precious metals for Republic National Bank in Hong Kong.
"The reaction is practically zero. I think Deng's death has been totally discounted by the gold market," the chief gold trader at a Singapore-based bank told Reuters.
Traditionally a safe haven for capital in times of political uncertainty, gold has lost much of its investment lustre in recent years as its price has stagnated in a narrow range.
Spot gold opened in Hong Kong on Thursday at US$344.60/345.10 an ounce, slightly below New York's previous $345.00/50 close overnight on Wednesday.
Price support was seen at between $344 to $342, while near-term resistance was pegged at $346 to $347 an ounce.
Dealers reported small amounts of profit taking, but market activity was quiet on Thursday with one Hong Kong trader saying players were reluctant to take positions in the morning session.
"The more important factor affecting the gold price is the U.S. dollar," said Anderson Cheung, chief bullion dealer for Swiss Bank Corp in Hong Kong.
The dollar briefly spiked higher overnight on Wednesday in what traders called a knee-jerk reaction to Deng's death.
Asian physical gold demand remained healthy with no abnormal activity noted in the markets, dealers said.

"We've had very strong physical demand over the last two weeks, but only because of the price being at these levels. There's been nothing more today to change that pattern," Republic's Gazmararian said.
Singapore-based precious metal traders said they were cheered by healthy physical demand for gold from buyers in China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Malaysia and Thailand.
"The demand from these countries is still pretty strong. They're buying kilobars and paying a high premium for it," one bank trader said.
Gold premiums were being quoted by regional dealers at around 120-150 U.S. cents an ounce over London spot prices, almost unchanged from last week's firm levels.
But if heavy buying continued, then premiums were expected to rally further, they said.
A shortage of gold bars for prompt delivery was also boosting Asian premiums quoted in the main distribution centres of Singapore and Hong Kong.
"There's no gold coming out of Australia and there's strong demand in South Korea," said a Hong Kong dealer.
Buyers in Thailand were also stocking up on gold due to domestic economic jitters and ahead of Tuesday's Bank of Thailand statement which ruled out any currency devaluation, a Singapore source said.
"People are buying gold because prices are low and some investors decided to get into precious metals to spruce up their portfolios," a Singapore bank analyst said.
Traders said the Hong Kong and Chinese stock markets, rather than bullion, were most sensitive to Deng's death.
Shanghai shares opened almost the 10 percent limit down on Thursday after Deng's death, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rebounded after initial weakness in morning trade.
